claim: The second movement of Haydn's symphony No. 94 begins with a string section creating the expectation of a gentle and soft piece, which is suddenly interrupted by a tutti fortissimo chord.
source: The second movement of Haydn's symphony No. 94 begins with a string section creating the expectation of a gentle and soft piece, which is suddenly interrupted by a tutti fortissimo chord.
evidence: This is a factual description of a musical composition that can be verified by examining the score or listening to the piece.

claim: Haydn's symphony No. 94 earned the nickname 'Surprise symphony' due to its startling motif.
source: This startling motif earned the composition the nickname 'Surprise symphony'.
evidence: This is a well-established historical fact about the naming of this musical composition.

claim: Music plays with listeners' expectations to evoke musical enjoyment and emotions.
source: All music, in fact, plays with listeners' expectations to evoke musical enjoyment and emotions, albeit often in more subtle ways (Huron, 2006; Juslin and Västfjäll, 2008; Meyer, 1957; Salimpoor et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Melody is a central element of music which induces musical expectations.
source: A central element of music which induces musical expectations is melody, the linear sequence of notes alternating in pitch.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text as a general principle about music.

claim: Within Western classical music, certain melodic patterns appear more frequently than others, establishing a musical syntax.
source: Within a musical piece and style, such as Western classical music, certain melodic patterns appear more frequently than others, establishing a musical syntax (Krumhansl, 2015; Patel, 2003; Rohrmeier et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on musical syntax.

claim: Human listeners continuously form predictions on how melody will continue based on musical regularities.
source: Human listeners have been proposed to continuously form predictions on how the melody will continue based on these regularities (Koelsch et al., 2019; Meyer, 1957; Tillmann et al., 2014; Vuust et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Higher surprise notes are rated as more unexpected by listeners.
source: Behaviorally, higher surprise notes are rated as more unexpected (Krumhansl and Kessler, 1982; Marmel et al., 2008; Marmel et al., 2010; Pearce et al., 2010; Schmuckler, 1989)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to behavioral studies.

claim: Higher surprise notes impair performance in dissonance detection tasks.
source: higher surprise notes are rated as more unexpected (Krumhansl and Kessler, 1982; Marmel et al., 2008; Marmel et al., 2010; Pearce et al., 2010; Schmuckler, 1989) and impair performance, for example in dissonance detection tasks (Pearce et al., 2010; Sears et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Listeners continue melodic primes with low-surprise notes in musical cloze tasks.
source: Listeners continue melodic primes with low-surprise notes in musical cloze tasks (Carlsen, 1981; Morgan et al., 2019; Schmuckler, 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Neural activity tracks melodic surprise.
source: Neural activity tracks melodic surprise (Di Liberto et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: High-surprise notes elicit the mismatch negativity electrophysiological signature.
source: high-surprise notes elicit electrophysiological signatures indicative of surprise processing, in particular the mismatch negativity (Brattico et al., 2006; Mencke et al., 2021; Näätänen et al., 2007; Quiroga-Martinez et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: High-surprise notes elicit the P3 component.
source: high-surprise notes elicit electrophysiological signatures indicative of surprise processing, in particular the mismatch negativity (Brattico et al., 2006; Mencke et al., 2021; Näätänen et al., 2007; Quiroga-Martinez et al., 2020) and P3 component (Quiroga-Martinez et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: High-surprise notes elicit the P2 component.
source: but also the P2 component (Omigie et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: High-surprise notes elicit a late negative activity around 400ms.
source: a late negative activity around 400ms (Miranda and Ullman, 2007; Pearce et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: High-surprise notes elicit changes in oscillatory activity.
source: and oscillatory activity (Omigie et al., 2019; Pearce et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The form and content of the internal model generating melodic expectations remain unclear.
source: Despite this extensive body of neural and behavioral evidence on the effects of melodic expectations in music perception, the form and content of the internal model generating these expectations remain unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Evidence on melodic expectations stems primarily from studying relatively artificial stimuli.
source: Furthermore, the evidence stems primarily from studying the processing of relatively artificial stimuli, and how these findings extend to a more naturalistic setting is unknown.
evidence: This is a characterization of the existing literature based on review of prior studies.

claim: Statistical learning models have proven slightly better fits for musical data than Gestalt-like models.
source: Overall, statistical learning models have proven slightly better fits for musical data (Temperley, 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Statistical learning models are better fits for human listeners' expectations assessed behaviorally than Gestalt-like models.
source: and for human listeners' expectations assessed behaviorally (Morgan et al., 2019; Pearce and Wiggins, 2006; Temperley, 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The two types of models (Gestalt-like and statistical learning) have rarely been directly compared.
source: but the two types of models have rarely been directly compared.
evidence: This is a characterization of the existing literature.

claim: The range of echoic memory is limited.
source: On the other hand, the range of echoic memory is limited and temporal integration windows are relatively short, especially in sensory areas (Hasson et al., 2008; Honey et al., 2012; Himberger et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Temporal integration windows are relatively short, especially in sensory areas.
source: On the other hand, the range of echoic memory is limited and temporal integration windows are relatively short, especially in sensory areas (Hasson et al., 2008; Honey et al., 2012; Himberger et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The Music Transformer is a state-of-the-art neural network model that can take long-range context into account more effectively than n-gram models.
source: To address this question, we derived model-based probabilistic estimates of expectations using the Music Transformer (Huang et al., 2018). This is a state-of-the-art neural network model that can take long-range (and variable) context into account much more effectively than the n-gram models previously used to model melodic expectations
evidence: This is a characterization of the Music Transformer model based on its architecture and citation to the original paper.

claim: Transformer models process blocks of musical context as a whole, instead of focusing on sequences of variable, yet limited, length.
source: since transformer models process blocks of (musical) context as a whole, instead of focusing on (note) sequences of variable, yet limited, length.
evidence: This is a description of how transformer models work based on established knowledge about their architecture.

claim: 35 participants underwent MEG recording while listening to diverse naturalistic compositions from Western classical music.
source: We then analyzed a newly acquired MEG dataset obtained while participants (n=35) were listening to diverse, naturalistic, musical stimuli using time-resolved regression analysis.
evidence: This describes the experimental data collected in the study.

claim: Neural activity over fronto-temporal sensors tracked melodic surprise particularly around 200ms and 300–500ms after note onset.
source: A time-resolved regression analysis revealed that neural activity over fronto-temporal sensors tracked melodic surprise particularly around 200ms and 300–500ms after note onset.
evidence: This is a finding from the MEG data analysis reported in the study.

claim: The neural surprise response was dissociated from sensory-acoustic and adaptation effects.
source: This neural surprise response was dissociated from sensory-acoustic and adaptation effects.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis showing that surprise effects are independent of other factors.

claim: Neural surprise was best predicted by computational models that incorporated long-term statistical learning rather than by simple, Gestalt-like principles.
source: Neural surprise was best predicted by computational models that incorporated long-term statistical learning—rather than by simple, Gestalt-like principles.
evidence: This is a main finding from comparing different computational models against neural data.

claim: The surprise reflected primarily short-range musical contexts of less than ten notes.
source: Yet, intriguingly, the surprise reflected primarily short-range musical contexts of less than ten notes.
evidence: This is a main finding from the context length analysis.

claim: Models taking longer-range context into account become better at predicting music, but worse at predicting neural activity, with a dissociation at about ten notes.
source: In particular, we observed a striking dissociation at a context window of about ten notes: models taking longer-range context into account become better at predicting music, but worse at predicting neural activity.
evidence: This is a main finding from comparing model performance on music versus neural data.

claim: Superior temporal cortical sources most strongly contributed to the surprise signature, primarily around 200ms and 300–500ms after note onset.
source: Superior temporal cortical sources most strongly contributed to the surprise signature, primarily around 200ms and 300–500ms after note onset.
evidence: This is a finding from the source localization analysis.

claim: The MEG findings were fully replicated in an independent openly available EEG dataset.
source: Finally, we present a full replication of our findings in an independent openly available EEG dataset (Di Liberto et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the replication analysis performed on independent data.

claim: The Onset model significantly explained variance in the recorded MEG data with mean r of 0.12 (SD = 0.03).
source: Unsurprisingly, this model significantly explained variance in the recorded MEG data (mean r across participants = 0.12, SD = 0.03; one-sample t-test versus zero, t34=25.42, p=1.06e-23, d=4.36, Figure 3A top left)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the MEG data analysis.

claim: The Baseline model explained additional variance beyond the Onset model (ΔrBaseline-Onset=0.013, SD = 0.006).
source: The Baseline model explained additional variance beyond the Onset model (ΔrBaseline-Onset=0.013, SD = 0.006; paired-sample t-test, t34=12.07, p=7.58e-14, d=2.07, Figure 3A bottom left)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the MEG data analysis.

claim: Differences in acoustic features and repetition modulated neural activity elicited by notes.
source: showing that differences in acoustic features and repetition further modulated neural activity elicited by notes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Baseline model results.

claim: All computational models of music performed significantly better than the Baseline model.
source: All models performed significantly better than the Baseline model, providing evidence for tracking of neural surprise during naturalistic music listening (Temperley: ΔrSurprise-Baseline=0.002, SD = 0.001, paired-sample t-test, t34=8.76 p=2.42e-09, d=1.5; IDyOM stm: ΔrSurprise-Baseline=0.001, SD = 0.001, t34=5.66 p=9.39e-06, d=0.97; IDyOM ltm: ΔrSurprise-Baseline=0.003, SD = 0.002, t34=12.74 p=2.51e-13, d=2.19; IDyOM both: ΔrSurprise-Baseline=0.002, SD = 0.001, t34=8.77, p=2.42e-09, d=1.5; and Music Transformer: ΔrSurprise-Baseline=0.004, SD = 0.002, t34=10.82, p=1.79e-11, d=1.86, corrected for multiple comparisons using the Bonferroni-Holm method)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the MEG data analysis comparing different models.

claim: The Music Transformer and IDyOM ltm model significantly outperformed the other models.
source: Importantly, the Music Transformer and IDyOM ltm model significantly outperformed the other models (paired-sample t-test, MT-Temperley: t34=7.56, p=5.33e-08, d=1.30; MT-IDyOM stm: t34=9.51, p=4.12e-10, d=1.63, MT-IDyOM both: t34=8.87, p=2.07e-09, d=1.52)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the MEG data analysis comparing different models.

claim: There was no statistically significant difference between the Music Transformer and IDyOM ltm model.
source: with no statistically significant difference between the two (paired-sample t-test, t34=1.634, p=0.225)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the MEG data analysis.

claim: The IDyOM stm model performed worst among the surprise models.
source: whereas the IDyOM stm model performed worst.
evidence: This is a comparison of model performance from the MEG data analysis.

claim: Listeners' melodic surprise is better explained by musical enculturation than by statistical regularities within the current musical piece alone or Gestalt-like rules.
source: These observations suggest that listeners' melodic surprise is better explained by musical enculturation (i.e., exposure to large amounts of music across the lifetime), modeled as statistical learning on a large corpus of music (IDyOM ltm and MT), rather than by statistical regularities within the current musical piece alone (IDyOM stm) or Gestalt-like rules (Temperley).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model comparison results.

claim: The Music Transformer model's surprise estimates predicted MEG data best at a context length of nine notes.
source: Strikingly, however, surprise estimates from the MT predicted MEG data best at a context length of nine notes and decreased for larger context lengths, even below the level of shorter ones (<10) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a result from the context length analysis on MEG data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Melodic expectations based on statistical learning rest on shorter time scales between 5 and 10 notes rather than long-range temporal structure.
source: Yet, melodic expectations based on statistical learning might not necessarily rest on long-range temporal structure but rather shorter time scales between 5 and 10 notes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the context length analysis results.

claim: The TRF for note onset was temporally extended from note onset up to 0.8 s in MEG.
source: The effect was temporally extended from note onset up to 0.8 s (MEG)
evidence: This is a result from the TRF analysis of MEG data.

claim: The TRF for note onset was temporally extended from note onset up to 1 s in EEG.
source: and 1 s (EEG)
evidence: This is a result from the TRF analysis of EEG data.

claim: The note onset effect clustered around bilateral fronto-temporal MEG sensors.

evidence: This is a statistical result from the spatial analysis of MEG data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The time course of the note onset TRF resembled a P1-N1-P2 complex.
source: The time course resembled a P1-N1-P2 complex, typically found in ERP studies on auditory processing (Picton, 2013; Pratt, 2011)
evidence: This is a characterization of the TRF based on comparison to known ERP components cited from prior research.

claim: The note onset TRF had a first positive peak at about 75ms (P1).
source: with a first positive peak at about 75ms (P1)
evidence: This is a result from the TRF analysis.

claim: The note onset TRF had a second positive peak at about 200ms (P2).
source: and a second positive peak at about 200ms (P2).
evidence: This is a result from the TRF analysis.

claim: The note onset TRF was followed by a sustained negative deflection between 300 and 600ms.
source: This was followed by a more sustained negative deflection between 300 and 600ms.
evidence: This is a result from the TRF analysis.

claim: A negative deflection at temporal sensors peaking at about 200ms was observed for note repetition, reflecting lower neural activity for repeated versus non-repeated notes.
source: We observed a negative deflection at temporal sensors peaking at about 200ms, reflecting lower neural activity for repeated versus non-repeated notes (MEG: p=5e-04, Figure 5B; EEG: p=0.008, Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the TRF analysis shown in Figures 5B and 6B.

claim: The repetition suppression effect extends to the setting of naturalistic music listening.
source: This extends the well-known auditory repetition suppression effect (Grill-Spector et al., 2006; Todorovic and de Lange, 2012) to the setting of naturalistic music listening.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the repetition results in the context of prior research.

claim: A fronto-temporal cluster of MEG sensors exhibited a positive peak at about 200ms for the surprise regressor.
source: Finally, the TRF of the surprise regressor indicates how the level of model-based surprise modulates neural activity over and above simple repetition. A fronto-temporal cluster of MEG sensors exhibited a positive peak at about 200ms
evidence: This is a result from the TRF analysis of the surprise regressor.

claim: A fronto-temporal cluster of MEG sensors exhibited a sustained negative deflection between 300 and 600ms for the surprise regressor.
source: and a sustained negative deflection between 300 and 600ms (MEG: p=5e-04, Figure 5C; EEG: p=0.004, Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the TRF analysis shown in Figures 5C and 6C.

claim: The increased activity for surprising notes is consistent with expectation suppression effects.
source: This finding is furthermore consistent with the more general effect of expectation suppression, the phenomenon that expected stimuli evoke weaker neural responses (Auksztulewicz and Friston, 2016; Garrido et al., 2009; Todorovic and de Lange, 2012; Wacongne et al., 2011)
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results in the context of prior research on expectation suppression.

claim: Expectation suppression occurs through gain modulation.
source: through gain modulation (Quiroga-Martinez et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation supported by citation to prior research.

claim: A sustained late negativity correlating with melodic surprise was found, which some studies have labeled a musical N400 or N500.
source: Additionally, we found a sustained late negativity correlating with melodic surprise, which some studies have labeled a musical N400 or N500 (Calma-Roddin and Drury, 2020; Koelsch et al., 2000; Miranda and Ullman, 2007; Painter and Koelsch, 2011; Pearce et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a result from the TRF analysis interpreted in the context of prior research.

claim: The N400 has been interpreted as an index of predictive music processing.
source: Similar to its linguistic counterpart (Kutas and Federmeier, 2011), the N400 has been interpreted as an index of predictive music processing.
evidence: This is a characterization of how the N400 has been interpreted in prior research.

claim: The mismatch negativity (MMN) and P3 component were not observed for melodic surprise in this study.
source: The literature has furthermore frequently emphasised the mismatch negativity (MMN) (Näätänen et al., 2007) and P3 component in predictive music processing (Koelsch et al., 2019), neither of which we observe for melodic surprise here.
evidence: This is a statement about what was not found in the data, contrasted with prior research.

claim: The MMN is typically found for deviants occurring in a stream of standard tones, such as in oddball paradigms.
source: However, the MMN is typically found for deviants occurring in a stream of standard tones, such as in oddball paradigms
evidence: This is a characterization of when the MMN is typically observed based on prior research.

claim: The P3 is usually observed in the context of an explicit behavioral task.
source: while the P3 is usually observed in the context of an explicit behavioral task (Koelsch et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a characterization of when the P3 is typically observed based on cited prior research.

claim: Listeners were listening passively to maximize the naturalistic setting.
source: In our study, listeners were listening passively to maximize the naturalistic setting, which could account for the absence of these components.
evidence: This describes the experimental design choice made in the study.

claim: The TRF peak deflection for the Onset regressor was best explained by sources in bilateral Heschl's gyri.
source: The TRF peak deflection for the Onset regressor was best explained by sources in bilateral Heschl's gyri (Figure 7, top).
evidence: This is a result from the source localization analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: The peak deflections for the Repetition and Surprise regressors were best explained by sources encompassing both bilateral Heschl's gyri as well as bilateral superior temporal gyri.
source: The peak deflections for the Repetition and Surprise regressors were best explained by slightly more lateral sources encompassing both bilateral Heschl's gyri as well as bilateral superior temporal gyri (see Figure 7 for exact MNI coordinates of density peaks).
evidence: This is a result from the source localization analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: The addition of uncertainty and its interaction with surprise did not improve but rather reduced models' cross-validated predictive performance on listeners' MEG data compared to surprise alone.
source: Surprisingly, the addition of uncertainty and its interaction with surprise did not further improve but rather reduce models' cross-validated predictive performance on listeners' MEG data compared to surprise alone (MT Surprise: ΔrSurpise-Baseline=0.004, SD = 0.002;+Uncertainty: ΔrUncertainty-Baseline=0.003, SD = 0.002, paired-sample t-test compared to Surprise, t34=–9.57, p=1.42e-10, d=–1.64;+Interaction S×U: ΔrSxU-Baseline=0.002, SD = 0.002, t34=–13.81, p=1.66e-14, d=–2.37) (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the analysis of uncertainty effects shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Melodic expectations have their origin in long-term exposure to the statistical structure of music.
source: To conclude, by using computational models to capture different hypotheses about the nature and source of melodic expectations and linking these to neural data recorded during naturalistic listening, we found that these expectations have their origin in long-term exposure to the statistical structure of music.
evidence: This is a main conclusion drawn from the overall pattern of results.

claim: As listeners continuously exploit long-term knowledge during listening, they do so primarily on the basis of short-range context.
source: Yet, strikingly, as listeners continuously exploit this long-term knowledge during listening, they do so primarily on the basis of short-range context.
evidence: This is a main conclusion drawn from the context length analysis results.

claim: Time-resolved regression used a time window from -0.2 s to 1 s relative to note onsets.
source: We constructed a time-expanded regression matrix M, which contained time-shifted versions of each regressor column-wise (tmin = –0.2 s, tmax = 1 s relative to note onsets, 73 columns per regressor given the sampling rate of 60 Hz).
evidence: This describes the parameters of the regression analysis.

claim: The risk for overfitting was low given the sparse design matrices and low correlations between the time-shifted regressors.
source: We instead opted to use OLS, since the risk for overfitting was low given the sparse design matrices and low correlations between the time-shifted regressors.
evidence: This is a justification for the methodological choice based on properties of the data.

claim: OLS (alpha = 0) was always among the best-fitting models when compared to ridge-regularized regression.

claim: A fivefold cross-validation scheme was applied to compare regression models' predictive performance.

evidence: This describes the cross-validation procedure used for model comparison.

claim: Channels most responsive to musical notes were selected for each participant according to the cross-validated performance for the Onset model (>2/3 quantile).
source: To increase the sensitivity of subsequent analyses, we selected the channels most responsive to musical notes for each participant according to the cross-validated performance for the Onset model (>2/3 quantile).
evidence: This describes the channel selection procedure for analysis.

claim: The approach controlled for overfitting the neural data and for differences in the number of regressors and free model parameters.
